takeaway: VectorCDC makes hashless content-defined chunking SIMD-friendly by vectorizing its extreme-byte search and range-scan primitives, reaching tens of gigabytes per second without changing chunk boundaries.
background: Deduplication divides input into chunks and removes repeated content. Content-defined chunking preserves boundaries across inserted or shifted bytes, but it scans every byte; hash-based schemes use rolling hashes, while hashless schemes choose boundaries from byte extrema.
villain: Rolling-hash state depends on the preceding byte, and an earlier vectorized design processes nonadjacent bytes with expensive gather/scatter instructions. Separating hashing from boundary selection also defeats minimum-chunk-size skipping, leaving only small speedups and no gain for FastCDC.
approach: VectorCDC expresses hashless CDC as two reusable operations. A reduction tree applies packed SIMD maxima or minima across fixed windows, and packed comparisons turn 64-byte range scans into masks whose first matching bit identifies a boundary. The authors instantiate the method for AE and RAM with SSE-128, AVX-256, and AVX-512.
impact: The paper exposes a compact algorithmic pattern for matching storage preprocessing to commodity CPU vectors. Because it preserves the native algorithms' boundary decisions, the throughput gain does not trade away deduplication effectiveness.

evaluation.overview: Experiments compare space savings, chunk-size distributions, and chunking throughput over five 40–230 GB versioned or snapshot datasets, several target chunk sizes, SIMD widths, two x86 platforms, and ablations of the two accelerated phases.
evaluation.implemented: The authors implement vectorized AE and RAM in about 700 lines of C++ and publish them through DedupBench. Implementations use SSE-128, AVX-256, or AVX-512 packed maximum/minimum and comparison operations without gather/scatter.
evaluation.setting: CloudLab machines include an AMD EPYC 7302P system with 16 cores and 128 GB RAM and an Intel Ice Lake system with two 32-core Xeon Silver 4314 CPUs and 256 GB RAM. Unless stated otherwise, runs use Ice Lake; each result averages five runs with under 5% standard deviation.

results.text: With AVX-512 and 8 KB chunks, vectorized RAM reaches 24–26 GB/s, which is reported as 21× faster than SS-Gear, 46× faster than SS-CRC, 16× faster than native RAM, and 12× faster than FastCDC.

SIMD acceleration produces the same chunk-size distributions and space savings as each native AE or RAM implementation; across all tested datasets and chunk sizes, native hashless savings remain within 6% of the hash-based algorithms.
Vectorized RAM reaches 13.3 GB/s with SSE-128 and 19.5 GB/s with AVX-256 and shows similar throughput on the tested AMD and Intel machines.

limitations: The evaluation measures the chunking kernel rather than an end-to-end deduplication service with hashing, index lookup, network transfer, and storage I/O. It covers five curated datasets and two x86 servers; portability beyond SSE/AVX, energy use, multi-core scaling, and production latency are not studied. The implementation evaluates AE and RAM and omits slower hashless algorithms such as MAXP. Hashless space savings can trail the best hash-based method, although the measured gap is at most 6%.
phd_group_signal: VectorCDC illustrates architecture-aware systems work at a deliberately small scope: identify common hot-loop primitives, redesign them around SIMD semantics, preserve functional equivalence, and validate across data characteristics, vector widths, and CPU vendors.

claims.text: Tree-based extreme-byte search repeatedly reduces packed adjacent bytes with SIMD maximum or minimum operations until only one vector remains, then scans that vector for the window extremum.

Packed range scanning compares 64 adjacent bytes with a replicated target under AVX-512, uses the comparison mask to locate the first qualifying byte, and retains minimum-chunk-size skipping after a boundary.
